q.intro.text: The graph of y equals x plus one, times x minus five, crosses the x-axis at minus one and at five. It is a parabola that opens up. Where is its lowest point? Pick an answer, and say how sure you are.

q.cb.right.text: At the start you picked two, minus nine, and you were right. Now you know why: halfway between the zeros, then the height there.

q.cb.yaxis.text: At the start you picked zero, minus five. That is where the graph crosses the y-axis. A parabola turns halfway between its zeros, at x equals two.

q.cb.zero.text: At the start you picked two, zero. The x was right, but the vertex is not on the x-axis: its height is f of two, which is minus nine.

q.cb.none.text: Zeros, then the axis halfway, then the height there. That finds the vertex of any parabola in factored form.

e.intro.text: Four steps. Press each one: the picture moves first, then the algebra.

e.step0.text: x plus one is zero at x equals minus one, and x minus five is zero at x equals five. A product is zero when one factor is zero, so the zeros are minus one and five.

e.step1.text: Both zeros have the same output, zero, so they are mirror images. The mirror line is halfway between them: minus one plus five, divided by two, is two. The axis of symmetry is x equals two.

e.step2.text: On the axis, x is two. y is two plus one, times two minus five: three times minus three, which is minus nine. The vertex is two, minus nine. The x squared term is positive, so the parabola opens up, and minus nine is the minimum.

e.step3.text: At x equals zero, y is one times minus five, which is minus five. Its mirror is as far on the other side of x equals two, at four, minus five. The curve goes through all of these. One function, three forms: factored, vertex form, and standard form.

e.why.text: Quick check: why is the axis exactly halfway between the zeros?

e.why.ok.text: Yes. Equal outputs come in mirror pairs, and the zeros are one such pair.

e.why.yaxis.text: Look at the picture: this one is centred on x equals two, not on the y-axis.

e.why.half.text: Three is half the distance. Start at minus one and go three: you land on two. Add the zeros and halve.

t.intro.text: Now y equals minus, x plus two, times x minus four. Its zeros are minus two and four.

t.axis.text: The axis of symmetry is halfway between the zeros. x equals what?

t.axis.ok.text: Yes: x equals one, halfway between minus two and four.

t.axis.no.text: Add the two zeros, then divide by two.

t.axis.half.text: Three is half the distance between them. Start at minus two and go three: add the zeros and halve.

t.axis.sign.text: The zeros are minus two and four, as they are. Minus two plus four, divided by two.

t.vertex.text: Put x equals one into the function. How high is the vertex?

t.vertex.ok.text: Yes: nine. The minus in front makes it open down, so one, nine is the highest point: a maximum.

t.vertex.no.text: Work out one plus two, times one minus four first, then apply the minus in front.

t.vertex.sign.text: One plus two, times one minus four, is minus nine. The minus in front flips it to nine.

t.vertex.zero.text: The vertex is not on the x-axis. Work out the function at x equals one.

t.int.text: Now the y-intercept: what is f of zero?

t.int.ok.text: Yes: eight. Its mirror across x equals one is two, eight. Now the curve fits through everything.

t.int.no.text: Put x equals zero in: minus, zero plus two, times zero minus four.

t.int.sign.text: Minus, two times minus four: two minus signs, so it is positive.

t.int.k.text: Nine is the vertex height. The y-intercept is the output at x equals zero.

p.intro.text: Sam checked f of x equals x minus three, squared, minus four, at x equals one and x equals five: both give zero. Sam says: equal outputs, two either side of three. That proves x equals three is the axis of symmetry. Has Sam proved it?

p.test.text: One pair matched. But there are infinitely many pairs. Prove it for all of them at once, with a general distance d.

p.build.text: Right: one pair is an example. Now prove it for every pair. Fill each because with the reason that makes the line true.

p.c1.text: Right. Three plus d minus three is d, so the square is d squared.

p.c2.text: Right. Minus d, squared, is d squared again.

p.c3.text: Right. Both sides are the same expression, for every d at once.

p.c4.text: Right. Every pair of inputs the same distance from three has the same output. That is a mirror line.

p.no.neg.text: Minus d times minus d is plus d squared. The minus signs cancel.

p.no.split.text: A function does not split over a sum. Put three plus d into the formula instead.

p.no.ex.text: One value of d is an example. The algebra has to hold for any d.

p.no.other.text: True, but it is the reason for a different line. Which reason makes this line true?

p.done.text: That is a proof: it holds for every distance d at once, not just the pair Sam checked. Sam's check was true, but it was an example.
